30.bp: When you search for movies or products online, the system shows you the top handful of results—not all 100,000 items ranked perfectly. What matters is whether those top 10 or top 20 are genuinely good for you. Recommender systems spend enormous energy trying to find the best few items quickly without having to rank the entire universe of choices.
30.wh: The obvious approach—rank everything and measure how good your top-K is—works mathematically but kills performance: you have to compute rankings for millions of items to know which ones are actually the best, which is slow and expensive. Second, user preferences shift over time (their taste changes, new items arrive), so even yesterday's ranking becomes stale and biased by old patterns. Building a loss function that directly optimizes top-K without computing full rankings is genuinely hard because top-K quality depends on relative positions, not absolute scores.
30.ap: Talos rewrites the ranking problem as a threshold problem: instead of 'rank items 1 to 100,000 then take the top 20,' the system asks 'what score would the 20th-best item have?' and then counts how many good items are above that threshold. This turns ranking into simple score comparisons. The system learns this threshold from data using a sampling trick, and adds a penalty term that stops the system from inflating scores (which would make the threshold meaningless). To handle shifting user preferences, they add a repair function that smooths out discontinuities and keeps the model stable as user behavior changes.
30.ww: Thresholds are much faster to compute than full rankings because you avoid sorting millions of items. The penalty for score inflation works because when scores climb too high, the threshold has to climb too, and the system gets no benefit—this creates a natural brake. The smoothing function protects against sudden user-behavior shifts because it lets the model make gradual adjustments rather than jerking to a new strategy instantly. These three ingredients working together turn an expensive ranking problem into a cheap threshold problem that stays stable over time.
30.po: The paper reports theoretical convergence proofs and experimental validation showing that Talos maintains accuracy while being far faster than existing approaches, and stays robust when user preferences shift—meaning the system can handle real-world conditions where recommendation rankings need to adapt constantly without breaking.

31.bp: Today's blockchain and cryptocurrency systems rely on a mathematical trick called public-key cryptography—you can lock something with one key (public) and only unlock it with a secret paired key (private). This protects billions of dollars of digital assets. Quantum computers, which recent breakthroughs have made increasingly practical, can break this trick entirely, making old-fashioned blockchains vulnerable to theft and fraud.
31.wh: Quantum computers don't run algorithms the way classical computers do; they exploit quantum weirdness to solve certain mathematical problems exponentially faster. The specific problems that guard public-key cryptography (factoring large numbers, solving discrete logarithm problems) are exactly what quantum computers excel at. Once a quantum computer exists, someone could retroactively unscramble old private keys from public blockchain data, stealing funds locked decades ago. No one has built a quantum computer strong enough to break cryptography yet, but the theoretical threat is immediate.
31.ap: This is a tutorial, not a research paper, so the approach is educational: it walks through how quantum computers work, why they threaten current blockchain security, and what defenses exist. The key defense is post-quantum cryptography—new mathematical puzzles that even quantum computers cannot solve quickly (often based on lattice problems or multivariate polynomials). The tutorial also covers quantum-assisted cryptography, where quantum properties themselves (quantum key distribution, entanglement) are used to make eavesdropping impossible. It shows how these fit into blockchain architectures and broader questions about privacy and trust in decentralized systems.
31.ww: Post-quantum algorithms are harder to break than factorization because even quantum computers cannot solve lattice problems efficiently—the quantum speedup doesn't apply. Quantum-assisted systems work because the laws of physics (quantum no-cloning, measurement collapse) prevent eavesdropping: if someone reads a quantum key, the key self-destructs and both sides know they were spied on. Educating the community now, before quantum computers become powerful, lets organizations transition gradually rather than facing a sudden cryptographic apocalypse.
31.po: The tutorial bridges lab theory (quantum computing breakthroughs) with real-world blockchain engineering (cryptographic standards, distributed consensus) and governance (data privacy, ethical accountability), giving technologists and policymakers a shared vocabulary to plan defenses before quantum computers threaten existing digital infrastructure.

32.bp: In remote regions without good roads or satellite coverage—parts of Africa, disaster zones after earthquakes, newly settled areas—nobody has built detailed digital maps of where people can actually move. Yet understanding human movement in these places matters for disaster response, urban planning, and public health. The only data available is often people's phones sporadically reporting location, with huge gaps and noise.
32.wh: Standard trajectory recovery (filling in the path between two GPS points) assumes you know the underlying road network; without it, you don't know whether someone walked straight through a forest or took a 10-kilometer detour. GPS signals themselves are unreliable in remote areas (trees, cloud cover, buildings), creating huge blank spots. Machine learning models trained on road-mapped regions (where data is clean) fail miserably when transferred to roadless regions because the patterns are fundamentally different. The data is sparse and unrepresentative, so the model has almost nothing to learn from.
32.ap: RHTR builds invisible 'maps' from historical movement data itself, without needing road data. It creates a multi-scale grid overlaid on each region—coarse grids capture global movement patterns (people generally move east or south), while fine grids capture local details (this specific cluster of points has narrow, winding movement). When someone's phone drops signal, the system looks at the surrounding region's patterns from that grid hierarchy and imagines what movement would fit. A coarse-to-fine reconstruction engine starts with the global pattern, then progressively refines the guess using local patterns, gradually filling in the missing segment step by step.
32.ww: Multi-scale grids work because human movement always has structure at multiple resolutions: large-scale patterns (regions tend to move toward markets or water), medium-scale patterns (neighborhoods have local routes), and fine-scale patterns (individuals navigate obstacles). Starting coarse prevents wild guesses; refining to fine detail keeps the guess realistic. Learning these patterns from observed data in each region means the model adapts to local geography without needing explicit maps. The system doesn't pretend to know roads; it learns movement regularities from what people actually did, which works even without infrastructure.
32.po: On two public datasets simulating remote and disaster scenarios, RHTR recovers missing trajectory segments more accurately than prior methods, even when training on data from completely different regions (cross-region transfer), because it learns the underlying movement structure rather than memorizing specific road networks.

33.bp: Decentralized finance (DeFi) lets anyone stake their money in blockchain liquidity pools—basically betting that prices will move in certain ways and earning fees if they're right. Small investors face a barrier: pools that deliver better returns demand large fund balances, so a person with $1,000 cannot compete with someone with $100,000, even if they both have equal skill. The question is: should small investors pool their money together to compete like one big fund, or stay fragmented?
33.wh: When many small investors compete separately, they each get worse returns because the protocol structure inherently favors larger funds (classic David vs. Goliath). But if they pool together, they become a giant force with monopoly-like power over the market, which might crush competition and hurt other investors. Game theory predicts that competing firms should eventually reach a balanced equilibrium where everyone does okay, but ranking-based DeFi breaks that prediction: monopoly actually delivers better returns than balanced competition, which contradicts textbook economics.
33.ap: The paper proves this mathematically using Stackelberg game theory (one player moves first, others respond), analyzing what happens when many investors choose to pool or stay separate. They model the revenue function as convex, meaning bigger pools benefit disproportionately from each additional dollar (economies of scale). They show that once asymmetry exceeds a critical threshold, the market will tip toward monopoly—small competitors cannot survive. To validate this, they run simulations on real Ethereum blockchain data, showing that different market starting conditions all converge to monopoly over time.
33.ww: Convex revenue functions mean that pooling is mathematically guaranteed to do better than competition: a $100,000 pool earns more than two $50,000 pools, not because collusion, but because of how the protocol's math works. Classical economics (Bertrand, Cournot) assumes linear or concave revenue functions, so those theories predict balanced competition. But when the revenue function has increasing returns to scale, those theories break. Once a pool gets slightly larger, it pulls in more money, which makes it even larger, creating a self-reinforcing spiral to monopoly.
33.po: Empirically, on real Ethereum data, funds aggregate into monopolistic structures regardless of initial conditions, and these monopolies actually achieve better outcomes for their members than fragmented competition would—a concrete demonstration that ranking-dependent DeFi protocols have built-in incentives toward concentration, contrary to what traditional competition theory predicts.

34.bp: Cloud services host thousands of applications serving millions of users simultaneously, all sharing the same network infrastructure. A video conference needs low latency; a backup job can tolerate delay; a real-time game needs guaranteed bandwidth. The system needs to juggle these competing demands—give each application exactly the bandwidth it needs, no more, no less, in real time.
34.wh: Traditional traffic control (Linux's Hierarchical Token Bucket) is static: you set rates once, and they never adapt. New cloud applications have highly dynamic demands—a video stream suddenly needs more bandwidth during high-motion scenes, then needs less during static scenes. The system has to sense this demand in real time and reallocate resources instantly. Building this efficiently is hard because checking and adjusting rates for thousands of flows billions of times per second would melt the CPU. Modern cloud systems offer only crude rate limiting (coarse-grained) that doesn't distinguish between priority levels.
34.ap: BeeQoS has three pieces: a high-speed data plane (using eBPF, special kernel-level code) that shapes each individual packet without slowing down; a control plane that constantly senses what bandwidth each flow actually needs right now (sampling real packets, not guessing); and Kubernetes integration so administrators can write policies in human language ('give video 20% bandwidth, backup gets leftovers'). When demand changes, the control plane recalculates allocation and the data plane instantly adjusts how much each packet is delayed before transmission. The system rebalances continuously, second by second.
34.ww: eBPF runs in the kernel so it shapes packets without context-switching to user-space code, which would be slow. Sampling real packets gives accurate demand signals because you measure what flows actually need, not what they claim. Adaptive reallocation works because the system checks demand often and adjusts smoothly rather than shocking flows with sudden rate changes. Kubernetes integration matters because operators already speak Kubernetes language; letting them express policies naturally means policies get deployed correctly.
34.po: Evaluation shows BeeQoS handles 1,000+ simultaneous flows while cutting median latency 72% and improving video quality-of-experience 27% versus traditional rate limiting, with stable performance and lower deployment overhead, because it dynamically matches bandwidth allocation to real-time application demands.

35.bp: When a video recommendation system keeps showing you videos from creators you already follow, you watch more (immediate engagement), but the platform becomes stale—emerging creators never get discovered, and you see the same people forever. Platforms want engagement, but also want a healthy ecosystem where new voices can grow. The tension is real: familiar content wins on engagement metrics, but suppresses diversity.
35.wh: Familiar content has an unfair advantage: you already trust it, so you click it faster. If the ranking system simply optimizes for clicks-per-item, it will naturally bury novel content, even if novel content would bring you joy if you tried it (you just need more proof). This is a structural bias built into the optimization metric, not user preference. Fixing it naively—say, always reserving 20% of rankings for novel content—hurts engagement and gets overridden by management pressure to maximize watch time.
35.ap: LAFB works after ranking is done (post-ranking stage), so it doesn't disrupt the main ranking system. It models how familiar you are with each content by analyzing your past interaction history with this creator or content type (how often you've watched them before). It computes personalized debiasing scores—essentially, multipliers that adjust your predicted interest in each video based on its novelty to you. Familiar videos get downweighted slightly; novel videos get upweighted slightly. The adjustment is personalized because someone who rarely watches creators might need different debiasing than a superfan.
35.ww: Applying debiasing at the post-ranking stage is safe: it doesn't break the main ranking pipeline or require retraining the main model, so it's low-risk to deploy. Personalized factors work because different users have different familiarity profiles—some are loyal-fans (should see less familiar stuff), others are explorers (can see slightly more novel stuff). The system preserves overall watch time by only deweighting gradually, so the adjustment doesn't feel jarring to users. Empirically, this small adjustment increases diversity without sacrificing engagement.
35.po: Deployed on YouTube, LAFB increased novel content watch-time share and expanded exposure for emerging creators while holding overall watch time stable and keeping user satisfaction steady—demonstrating that diversity and engagement are not mutually exclusive if you apply the right adjustment at the right stage.

36.bp: Group chats on social platforms are where people ask questions, solve problems together, and share interests. But many group chats die out (inactivity), or take chaotic turns, or lack structure. If you could add smart AI agents to the chat that encourage good discussion, answer questions helpfully, or playfully challenge the group, you could revive engagement and make chats more valuable without a human moderator working 24/7.
36.wh: Large language models work great in one-on-one conversation where context is simple and stable. Group chat is fundamentally messier: multiple people talk over each other, context shifts rapidly, a single user's tone is hard to infer, and inserting a bot can feel intrusive or break the conversational flow. The system needs to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. It needs to coordinate multiple agent personalities without confusing users. Existing LLM systems treat multi-party chat as 'extend the conversation,' but real group chat needs active management—when to trigger an agent, which agent, how to blend its response into the human flow.
36.ap: GCAgent has three components: an Agent Builder that customizes agents to match group interests (personality, expertise, tone); a Dialogue Manager that tracks conversation state, decides when agents should speak up, and prevents awkward interruptions or redundant comments; and Interface Plugins that reduce friction for users to invoke or configure agents (three specific tools for interaction). The system lets groups define 'entertainment' agents (funny, engaging) and 'utility' agents (answering factual questions, summarizing), which operate under different speaking rules. The dialogue manager essentially watches the chat flow and decides: 'This is the right moment for the expert agent to jump in' or 'Stay silent, humans are handling this.'
36.ww: Customizing agents to group interests means the voice fits the existing chat culture, so it feels invited rather than intrusive. Dialogue state tracking prevents the system from speaking out of turn or repeating itself, which would derail conversation. Separate entertainment and utility agents work because they operate under different logic—entertainment agents are bold and speak frequently, while utility agents are cautious and only activate when needed. Interface plugins reduce friction because users don't have to write code or formulate perfect prompts to use agents; they can summon them with one click.
36.po: In 350 days of real-world deployment, GCAgent increased message volume 28.8% and achieved 4.68/5 average rating, preferred by users 51% of the time versus the base model—showing that well-timed, well-integrated agents can revive group activity and enhance conversation quality without feeling intrusive.

37.bp: Graph learning is about predicting properties of networks—which users will connect, which nodes matter most, whether two nodes belong in the same group. The assumption has always been 'similar nodes link to each other' (homophily, like your friends are similar to you). But real networks often violate this: in citation networks, papers can cite very different papers; in social networks, people disagree with their friends. Building a single foundation model that works on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs is the frontier.
37.wh: Most graph models assume homophily and exploit it: if your neighbors are similar to you, then your neighbors' features tell you about your own features. On heterophilic graphs this breaks catastrophically—your neighbors are different from you, so copying their feature patterns makes you less similar to them, causing the model to predict you wrongly. The deeper problem is that homophily and heterophily don't exist at one granularity; they exist at multiple scales. A node overall might be homophilic (similar neighbors), but some individual feature dimensions might be heterophilic (your neighbors' color differs from yours), and vice versa. Existing methods check only at node level and miss these fine-grained patterns.
37.ap: TFSGFM (Topology-aware Feature Sorting Graph Foundation Model) looks at homophily and heterophily at the fine granularity of individual features, not entire nodes. For each feature of each node, it asks: 'Are my neighbors' values for this feature similar to or different from mine?' It then sorts features based on these per-feature topology patterns. A dual-channel architecture processes the sorted features: one channel for homophilic features (similar), one for heterophilic features (different). Each channel uses different aggregation rules—homophilic features copy neighbor values, heterophilic features contrast against neighbor values. The system learns which features belong in which channel and combines them.
37.ww: Feature-level sorting works because it captures a reality that node-level sorting misses: within a single node, some dimensions follow homophily and some follow heterophily. Different aggregation rules for different feature types prevent the fundamental mistake of averaging features that shouldn't be averaged. The dual-channel architecture naturally handles both graph types using the same foundation model, because it adapts the aggregation strategy per feature rather than per graph. This enables one model to work across diverse graph structures without retraining.
37.po: Experiments demonstrate that TFSGFM handles both homophilic and heterophilic graphs in a unified framework, outperforming methods designed specifically for one type, and even on homophilic graphs it better exploits the small heterophilic signals that exist—proving that feature-level topology awareness gives foundation models more flexibility and accuracy.

38.bp: Modern web applications spread across dozens of microservices—each service handles one job (payment, recommendations, notifications), and they call each other. When something breaks (payment service gets slow, recommendation service crashes), finding the root cause is like debugging a 100-layer telephone game. Engineers trace requests as they bounce between services, but interpreting traces requires deep expertise and takes hours. Automating trace analysis would catch problems in minutes.
38.wh: Trace analysis is hard because traces are unstructured: a single trace might involve 50 services, each logging in different formats, and the interesting patterns—'service A always delays after service B returns 503'—are buried in thousands of log lines. Existing trace analysis tools require manual rules ('if latency > 500ms, trigger alert'), which miss unexpected failure modes. Large language models could help here because they understand natural language patterns, can reason about chains of events, and can generalize across different services without reprogramming. But LLM capabilities for trace analysis have never been systematically evaluated, and it's unclear what level of fine-tuning is needed.
38.ap: The paper first builds TraceBench, a benchmark dataset of traces with labeled analysis tasks (detect anomaly, identify root cause, predict latency). They then evaluate existing LLMs on this benchmark to see which models are naturally good at trace reasoning. They find LLMs have potential but room to improve, so they propose TraceLLM: taking an LLM and fine-tuning it on TraceBench tasks. The fine-tuning teaches the model to parse traces, recognize causal patterns, and output diagnoses in standardized format. They compare against open-source and closed-source baselines.
38.ww: Fine-tuning works because LLMs already have strong reasoning skills from general pretraining; they just need to learn the specific trace domain (vocabulary, patterns, output format). Traces are semi-structured text, which LLMs handle naturally. Building a benchmark first (TraceBench) lets them measure progress and understand which tasks are hard, so they can focus fine-tuning on the bottlenecks. Generalizing across services works because trace patterns are somewhat universal (latency cascades, resource exhaustion, failures propagating) even though implementations differ.
38.po: Fine-tuned TraceLLM outperforms open-source LLMs by 34.77% average accuracy on trace analysis tasks and beats closed-source baselines, demonstrating that LLMs with domain-specific tuning can automate a task that currently requires expert human time and reduces mean time to diagnosis in microservice systems.

39.bp: E-commerce platforms and streaming services track what you watch or buy across multiple services you use—shopping, streaming video, social network, music. Recommenders could use this cross-domain history to give better suggestions. Someone who buys sci-fi books might enjoy sci-fi films; someone who listens to jazz might enjoy jazz documentaries. But user histories are sparse—you buy rarely, watch intermittently—so combining data from multiple domains should provide more signal to learn from.
39.wh: Naive cross-domain recommendation fails in time-aware scenarios. Suppose I stopped watching sci-fi movies six months ago but just started reading sci-fi books. A simple transfer would predict I love sci-fi films, but I've moved on. The time dimension matters: old interactions age out, new interactions have more weight. Also, the optimal timing to transfer information is different for different users: a fast-moving trendsetter wants recent data; a loyal user wants long-term history. Ignoring timing and treating all history equally causes transfer learning to backfire. Current cross-domain methods assume interactions are uniformly spread in time, which is unrealistic.
39.ap: TA-CDSR (Time-Aware Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation) has three pieces: (1) Time-sensitive attention that splits your interaction sequence into 'what items did you interact with' and 'when did you interact with them,' treating these separately so the model learns both the items you like and the temporal pattern of your interests; (2) A preference generator that uses source-domain interactions and their timestamps to reconstruct what your target-domain interactions would look like if your interests were consistent across domains, but weighted by time so recent source interactions influence the guess more; (3) Multi-scale time windows that measure how dense your interactions are at different time scales (hourly, daily, monthly) and dynamically adjust how much cross-domain knowledge to transfer based on this density.
39.ww: Decoupling items and time works because interest changes over time, and the model needs to track both independently. Weighting by time lets the model realize 'you were into sci-fi six months ago but aren't now, so this shouldn't influence your film recommendation.' Multi-scale windows adapt to personal rhythms: someone who shops daily should see recent-only history; someone who shops monthly should look further back. Adaptively weighting cross-domain transfer by interaction density means the system transfers knowledge when domains are rich in data and relies on target-domain data when it's rich and sources are sparse.
39.po: Experiments on three real-world datasets show TA-CDSR achieves competitive computational efficiency while outperforming baselines, because temporal structure allows it to extract signal from cross-domain history without being misled by outdated preferences.

40.bp: Blockchain networks are under attack: criminals use them to hide stolen money, launder drug proceeds, or ransom victims. Regulators and exchanges need to identify malicious addresses in real time. The problem is scale—billions of transactions, millions of addresses—and the adversaries adapt constantly. A model trained on last year's fraud patterns will miss this year's new schemes. Transfer learning (applying knowledge from previously identified fraud to new fraud) should work because fraud is fraud, but the complex nature of blockchain data (graph structure, price history, message text) makes transfer hard.
40.wh: Blockchain fraud changes constantly: money laundering that worked last month gets detected, so criminals invent new techniques. A model trained on old fraud will not recognize new patterns. The data itself is multi-modal and noisy—transaction graphs show connections between addresses, temporal sequences show wash trading patterns, price history shows market manipulation, and textual metadata describes transactions. Each modality tells a different story, and good fraud detection needs all of them. Existing transfer learning methods for graphs ignore temporal and textual data, and methods that use all three modalities don't transfer well across blockchains because distributions shift (different blockchain = different users, different fraud ecology).
40.ap: MOE-GTL (Multi-mOdal Enhanced Graph Transfer Learning) combines three modalities: (1) Graph structure, encoded as a network of addresses and connections; (2) Temporal sequences, capturing how transaction volume and price change over time; (3) Textual features describing transaction metadata. The model learns representations in each modality separately, then learns how to combine them. The key innovation is distribution alignment: the model explicitly corrects for the fact that source and target blockchains have different fraud patterns and user populations by learning a transformation that maps source distribution to target distribution. This learned transformation enables knowledge from old fraud to apply to new fraud.
40.ww: Multi-modal learning works because different fraud types leave different fingerprints: structural fraud (circular money transfers) shows in the graph; temporal fraud (sudden price spikes) shows in sequences; textual fraud (suspicious message content) shows in metadata. Learning to combine these modalities gives the model more signal. Distribution alignment works because the core fraud mechanics (circular transfers, price manipulation) are shared across blockchains; the distribution shift is mostly in the user base and transaction volume, which the alignment layer can correct. Transfer learning then applies successfully because the aligned representations encode generalizable fraud patterns.
40.po: MOE-GTL detects fraud in emerging blockchain networks by transferring knowledge from previous fraud cases, handling the multi-modal and dynamic nature of blockchain data through simultaneous graph, temporal, and textual reasoning with distribution-aware transfer, enabling faster detection of new fraud schemes without waiting to accumulate labeled data in each new blockchain.

41.bp: Cloud platforms run thousands of microservices in a data center, each serving users from different services (payment, analytics, user profile, notifications). Each service has dependencies: payment service calls user database; analytics depends on event logging; the system needs to forecast CPU, memory, and latency. If forecasts are accurate, the platform can allocate resources ahead of demand and avoid outages.
41.wh: Naive forecasting treats each service independently, but microservices are interconnected in complex ways: if user-database load spikes, every service that queries it will suffer. The connections form a graph, but the graph is not a static blueprint—connections are dynamic, activated only when services call each other. Furthermore, within each microservice, there are causal chains: workload first drives CPU usage, which drives memory usage, which drives latency. A spike in workload cascades through these causal chains. Existing forecasting methods ignore one or both layers (the graph of service dependencies, and the causal chains within each service), so they miss crucial signal.
41.ap: MaMiClif (macro-micro collaborative learning) models both layers: (1) Macro (service-level): constructs a graph where nodes are services, edges represent dependencies, and weights capture interaction strength. It uses heterogeneous graph convolution, which updates representations by mixing information from different types of edges (collaborative, backup, dynamic). (2) Micro (indicator-level): constructs a matrix showing which performance metrics (workload, CPU, memory, latency) causally affect each other within a service. It uses causal self-attention, a variant of attention that weights relationships by measured causal strength (e.g., workload has stronger causal influence on latency than memory does). The forecast combines both by first predicting service-level workload using the macro graph, then predicting individual metrics using the micro matrix conditioned on the macro predictions.
41.ww: Heterogeneous graph convolution handles multiple edge types because different dependencies (collaborative vs. backup) behave differently; one edge type should not overshadow the others. Causal self-attention works because causality is asymmetric (workload causes latency, not vice versa), and explicitly weighting by causal strength prevents the model from learning spurious correlations. Combining macro and micro predictions works because top-down (graph) and bottom-up (causal) reasoning reinforce each other: the macro prediction provides boundary conditions, the micro chains fill in detailed mechanics.
41.po: Experiments on data center workloads show MaMiClif forecasts microservice metrics more accurately than baselines by jointly modeling service dependencies and intra-service causality, enabling better resource allocation and reduced risk of outages.

42.bp: Meme coins (joke cryptocurrencies like Dogecoin) are traded obsessively and have become a $100+ billion market. Many investors use copy-trading bots—they watch expert traders and automatically copy their trades. But meme coin markets are thin and manipulable, and adversaries deploy bots to front-run (trade ahead of you), fake enthusiasm (fabricate positive sentiment), and extract money from naive copiers. Building a system to detect manipulation and protect copiers is urgent.
42.wh: Copy trading is inherently adversarial: your trades signal information (you think the price will go up), and adversaries can exploit this signal by trading ahead of you and dumping at a higher price once they've benefited. Traditional fraud detection uses statistics (sudden price spikes, volume anomalies), but sophisticated bots adapt: they learn what patterns trigger detection and avoid them. A copier cannot trust price data alone because prices reflect manipulation. The challenge is to predict trader profitability not from price signals, but from the broader behavioral and market context.
42.ap: The paper builds a multi-agent defense system using a multimodal LLM and chain-of-thought reasoning. Instead of detecting bots by pattern matching, it reasons about trader behavior end-to-end: (1) A multimodal LLM processes multiple signals—transaction history, sentiment data from social media, trade timing, market conditions—to form a rich picture of what the trader was thinking; (2) Chain-of-thought reasoning makes the LLM articulate its reasoning step-by-step ('trader bought before announcement, sold after spike, which suggests advance knowledge'), revealing manipulation; (3) The system predicts whether following this trader is profitable, accounting for the adversarial environment. The approach outperforms statistics-based detection because it reasons about intent and market microstructure.
42.ww: Chain-of-thought reasoning works because manipulation leaves behavioral signatures—timing anomalies, message patterns, correlated trades—that an LLM can recognize and articulate. Multimodal input (prices + social sentiment + transactions) prevents adversaries from gaming any single signal; manipulating all modalities simultaneously is harder. Predicting profitability directly (rather than detecting bots) frames the problem correctly: the copier cares whether following this trader makes money, and the LLM can assess this by reasoning about adversarial context.
42.po: In realistic meme coin markets with substantial friction, the multi-agent LLM system achieves 3% average return per investment, outperforming zero-shot LLM predictions and statistical baselines in both accuracy and economic performance—demonstrating that reasoning-based defenses can make copy trading viable even in adversarial, manipulated markets.

43.bp: Vast amounts of structured data live on the web—product catalogs (electronics, prices, descriptions), knowledge bases (facts about entities), scientific datasets (measurements, metadata). These tables are heterogeneous and messy, making it hard to build a single classification model ('is this item electronics or clothing?'). Large language models are already deployed everywhere, so if you could reuse their semantic understanding (the knowledge they already extracted from text), you might avoid training specialized models on each table.
43.wh: LLMs produce semantic embeddings—numerical summaries of text meaning—but these embeddings are optimized for text retrieval and language understanding, not for table classification. A naive approach would pass a table row as text to an LLM, get an embedding, and classify it, but this underperforms specialized tabular models that exploit table structure. The question is: why don't embeddings work well, and can we fix them without retraining the LLM? LLMs are black boxes; you cannot easily modify them. The path forward requires understanding what LLM embeddings are missing for tabular tasks.
43.ap: TaRL (Table Representation with Language Model) uses LLM embeddings directly but applies two fixes: (1) Remove the common component—across all embeddings in a batch, there is often a direction where embeddings are similar (called a 'dominant direction'). This common component wastes the embedding space; subtracting it out leaves more room for meaningful differences between items. (2) Calibrate softmax temperature—the softmax function converts scores into probabilities using a temperature parameter. LLM embeddings often need a different temperature than default to produce good probabilities for classification. A simple meta-learner, trained on handcrafted features, learns to predict the right temperature for each table. This approach uses minimal additional training (only the temperature predictor, not the LLM).
43.ww: Removing the common component works because it frees up the embedding space: if all embeddings point in the same direction, the classifier cannot see differences. Subtracting the mean/dominant direction is a standard technique in representation learning. Calibrating temperature works because LLM embeddings come from language training, where temperature matters differently than in tabular classification; adjusting it for the new task is a form of domain adaptation. The meta-learner is lightweight because it only predicts one scalar (temperature), not hundreds of weights, so it trains quickly on small labeled datasets.
43.po: TaRL achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art specialized tabular models on few-shot classification tasks using only LLM embeddings and two post-hoc corrections, demonstrating that deployed LLMs can be repurposed for structured data without specialized retraining or model modification.

44.bp: Teachers spend hours planning lessons—deciding learning objectives, choosing teaching methods, designing activities, preparing assessments. Lesson plans that work are often inconsistent in structure and rarely adapt in real time to student needs. Automating lesson planning would free up teacher time and let plans adapt to different learners. Large language models could help, but a single LLM often produces generic plans. Multiple LLMs with different expertise, collaborating, might produce better plans.
44.wh: A novice teacher knows the big picture but struggles with specifics (how exactly do I teach photosynthesis?). An experienced teacher knows the curriculum deeply but might miss pedagogical innovation. A pedagogical expert understands how learning works but might not know your specific curriculum. Getting one LLM to do all three roles causes it to make compromises, producing mediocre plans. The insight is that lesson planning is inherently collaborative—you need multiple perspectives, and the perspectives must argue and refine. Existing approaches use a single LLM or chain-of-thought, which lacks true collaboration.
44.ap: COMA (Collaborative Multi-Role Agent) deploys three specialized agents: (1) Novice agent—understands the lesson topic but lacks precision; proposes a rough lesson flow; (2) Veteran agent—deeply knows the curriculum and textbooks; critiques and refines the flow, filling in knowledge details; (3) Master agent—exhibits pedagogical expertise; redesigns activities to adapt to diverse learners, adds assessment strategies. The agents iterate: novice proposes, veteran refines, master polishes. This mimics how real educational teams work. Each agent is a separate LLM instance with custom prompts that emphasize its role's perspective.
44.ww: Iterated collaboration works because each agent catches what others miss and proposes corrections. The novice grounds the plan in content; the veteran ensures accuracy; the master ensures pedagogy. Having explicit roles prevents agents from converging to mediocrity; each agent defends its perspective. Iterations allow agents to build on each other: veteran refines novice, master refines veteran, novice may refine master on content details. This dance produces plans that integrate multiple viewpoints rather than averaging them out.
44.po: Comprehensive experiments across five subjects using expert-designed pedagogical metrics show COMA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline LLM methods, producing lesson plans that are more structured, coherent, and adaptable to diverse learner needs—demonstrating that multi-agent collaboration is more effective than single-agent generation for complex knowledge work requiring multiple expertise.
